newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania scrambles to meet reform targets for loans.
newsitem.headline: Romania scrambles to meet reform targets for loans.

text.p: Romania's reformist government scrambled on Thursday to meet reform targets and win Western credits, presenting new legislation and announcing accelerated targets for privatisation and restructuring industry.

With the International Monetary Fund's chief negotiator meeting ministers and the World Bank examining a credit package, the government announced critical new investment rules and pledged to speed up plans to overhaul industry.
It also pledged to action to dismantle the giant loss-making "regimes autonomes" running strategic sectors of industry and public utilities.

And its main privatisation agency pledged to press on with plans to turn more than a hundred firms over to private hands, some through foreign stock exchanges. At least 100 more would be sold off, it said, with World Bank assistance.

In Washington, the World Bank announced approval of $550 million in loans to help restructure the farming sector, upgrade potholed roads and cushion consumers hit hardest by price liberalisation and falling living standards.
Romanians' average monthly wages stand at less than $80.

But the Bank's resident representative in Bucharest, Francois Ettori, said the resumption of at least $80 million in credits to restructure industry had been put off until the end of the week for "technical reasons".

Ettori told state television Romania had to meet certain conditions for further loans -- privatisation of 850 firms by the end of 1997, including 50 large factories, the sale of two state banks and closure of persistent loss-making firms.
Ministers in the government, which ousted ex-communists in last year's general election, pledged quick, firm action.
Reform Minister Ulm Spineanu emerged from a cabinet meeting announcing plans to subdivide unwieldy state utilities and create more profitable "companies of national interest".
"This is a major move for reforms and a big change in our economy," he said.

A decree outlining investment legislation sought to soothe investors who had long complained of an absence of clear rules. It set a capital gains repatriation tax of four percent, far lower than initial proposals.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea formally sought parliament's support for the reform programme this week. The two chambers are expected later this week to turn back without difficulty a confidence vote moved by the leftists now in opposition.

The government has already passed a tough budget aimed at trimming monthl-on-month inflation -- which peaked at 30.7 percent in March -- to two percent by the end of the year and reducing bulging budget and current account deficits.

Government ministers and Western lenders accuse the ousted left-wing administration of hindering reforms in the seven years it held power after the 1989 execution of communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Both the IMF and the World Bank suspended credits last year, complaining that the government of the time had overspent and failed to meet reform targets.
